newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bolger unwilling to trade away NZ tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Bolger unwilling to trade away NZ tax cuts.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger said he would be "most reluctant" to scrap next year's planned second round of tax cuts in horse-trading following next Saturday's general election.
Bolger said in a Sunday night television interview: "I'm not going to trade anything that takes New Zealand backwards."

He said his conservative National Party was fully committed to an adequately funded health service and would not scrap the Employment Contracts Act deregulating the labour market, although it might be prepared to look at the wording of individual clauses.
"Tearing up the Employment Contracts Act is not on for us," Bolger said.

Asked if he would be prepared trade off the second round of tax cuts in favour of extra funding for health, Bolger said many trades would have to be considered in negotiations on coalition-forming after the election.
But he added: "I would be very reluctant, most reluctant, to give away tax cuts."

Bolger said it was not a "reasonable proposition" to suggest he might be asked to step aside in the interests of forming a coalition between National and economic nationalist New Zealand First, whose leaders have said they could not work with him or Finance Minister Bill Birch.
He did not expect his party to "toss me out".

Bolger reiterated that the left-wing Alliance would set a high price for being part of a coalition with Labour and New Zealand First, and its policies would lead to higher taxes, higher interest rates, stronger trade unions and fewer jobs.
He denied National could be held hostage by its own potential coalition partners such as radical free-market Act New Zealand and made to back policies such as privatisation of health and education.
Bolger said Act would be a small party, if it made it into parliament at all, and in no position to dictate anything.

A TVNZ opinion poll earlier on Sunday showed National down six points to 34 percent, while Labour climbed the same amount to 24 percent. New Zealand First and the Alliance were both on 15 percent. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 471-4277
